questions.Q1: To start, tell me a bit about your work: what do you do, in what field, and roughly how many years you've been working?
questions.Q2: How does artificial intelligence show up in your job today, if at all? Are you using any AI tools, and how is it changing your work?
questions.Q3: Thinking about growing your skills, have you taken any courses or training in the last few years? What would make you invest your own time or money in learning something new, and what's held you back before?
questions.Q4: What's your honest first reaction to that? What stands out, good or bad?
questions.Q5: How well does something like this fit your situation and your goals? Is it for someone like you?
questions.Q6: Do you believe a course like this would actually help you use AI well in your work? And does it matter to you that the certificate comes from a university?
questions.Q7: You can already find a lot of AI training online, some of it free, and your employer may offer some. What, if anything, would make a paid university program worth it over those options?
questions.Q8: Thinking about the format, 8 weeks, one live evening a week, and around four to five hours a week total, how does that fit your life? Would that work for you?
questions.Q9: Do you think finishing something like this would actually help your career, your earning power, or your job security?
questions.Q10: The course is pitched as a way to 'stay ahead as AI reshapes your field, rather than get left behind.' Does that framing land for you, or would a different angle be more appealing?
questions.Q11: Before I tell you, what would you expect a program like this to cost? [Then revealed: This program costs $3,000. What's your reaction to that price? Does it feel worth it for what's offered?]
questions.Q12: Would you expect to pay for this yourself, have your employer cover it, or split it? And how does that change how you feel about it?
questions.Q13: What would stop you from actually enrolling in something like this?
questions.Q14: Being honest, how likely would you be to seriously consider enrolling in this? And why?
questions.Q15: Last one: what single change would make you much more likely to enroll, or what's missing for you?

v.Q2:
Honestly, AI is pretty woven into how I work at this point. I use ChatGPT a lot — like almost every day — for things like drafting vendor communications, summarizing long email threads, and generating first drafts of project status reports that I then edit down. I've also started using Notion AI for meeting notes and to pull action items out of call recordings, which has saved me a surprising amount of time. And we recently got access to Copilot through our Microsoft 365 subscription, so I've been experimenting with that for Excel work, mostly building formulas and doing quick data cleanup.

There's definitely a pressure, even if no one says it outright, to be the person on the team who knows this stuff. Our operations director has mentioned a few times that she wants us to document how we're using AI tools so the rest of the team can replicate it. So I kind of feel like I've been handed an informal mandate to figure it out and evangelize it, which is fine by me. I'm genuinely excited about where it's going, though I do think some of my colleagues are more anxious than I am. I feel pretty good about where I sit right now, but I'm aware that the tools are changing fast enough that I can't just coast on what I know today.
v.Q3:
Yeah, I've done a few things. I completed a PMP prep course a couple of years ago, self-funded, and I've done a handful of LinkedIn Learning paths — mostly on Agile and data literacy — which my employer covered. I also did a short Google Analytics certification that I just knocked out on my own time.

What makes me invest is pretty clear in my head: it has to feel directly applicable to what I'm doing or want to do next, not just theory. The PMP stuff was great because it had a concrete credential at the end and I knew it would signal something to employers. The LinkedIn Learning stuff was hit or miss honestly — some of it was useful, a lot of it felt like content for content's sake.

The real barrier for me is time, and I think relevance is close behind. I've started things and abandoned them when they stopped feeling connected to a real outcome. I also find it hard to carve out focus time when I'm primarily remote, because the boundaries between work and not-work are kind of blurry. If something has a schedule and a cohort and actual deadlines, I'm more likely to finish it than if it's just sitting there as a self-paced option.
v.Q4:
My first reaction is pretty positive, I think. What stands out immediately is the hands-on framing — working on actual projects from your own job rather than generic exercises. That's the thing that always separates training that sticks from training that doesn't, in my experience. The no-coding requirement is also worth calling out because that removes a mental barrier a lot of people have, including some of my colleagues who I think would benefit from this kind of thing but assume it's not for them.

The evening format is interesting — I could see that working well for people who have structured workdays, though for me being remote it's a little more flexible. The eight-week length feels right. Long enough to actually go somewhere, short enough that it doesn't feel like a second job. I guess the one thing I want to know more about is how current the tool stack is, because AI tools evolve fast enough that a course built six months ago could already feel dated. But overall, honestly, this is the kind of thing I'd look at seriously.
v.Q5: I'd say it fits maybe seventy percent of the way. The role-based framing — operations, marketing, HR — that's me. The practical application angle is me. The professional certificate piece is something I value. Where I pause a little is that I'm already a fairly active user, so I want to make sure there's enough depth that I'm not just covering ground I've already covered on my own. If it's really designed for people who are starting from zero, I might find the early weeks slow. But if there's enough in there about building more systematic workflows or using AI across a team, rather than just individual productivity tricks, then yes, it's absolutely for someone like me.
v.Q6:
I do believe it could help, with the caveat I just mentioned about depth. The project-based format is genuinely the right way to learn applied tools, so structurally I think it's set up to work. Whether it actually delivers depends a lot on the instructor and how current the content is — those are the variables I can't assess from a description alone.

The university credential does matter to me, and I think more than I would have expected a few years ago. Partly it's the signal it sends externally — a certificate from a recognizable institution carries more weight on a resume than a Udemy badge. But also, I kind of trust that a university is going to put some rigor into the curriculum design in a way that a random online platform might not. It's not a magic bullet, but it's a meaningful signal.
v.Q7:
So I've consumed a lot of free content — YouTube channels, Reddit deep-dives, the Microsoft Copilot documentation, various free courses. And I think the honest answer is that free content is great for picking up individual tactics but really bad at giving you a coherent framework. You end up knowing a bunch of tricks but not really understanding how to think about where AI fits into a workflow systematically.

What a structured program does is force you to build that framework, and having live sessions where you can ask questions and see how other professionals are applying it — that's genuinely valuable. The credential is also something free content can never give you. My employer does offer some training through our L&D platform, but it's pretty surface level and not really designed for someone who wants to go deep. So the differentiation for me is structure, cohort accountability, and the credential. If this program delivers all three, I think the paid model justifies itself.
v.Q8: Four to five hours a week is manageable. Eight weeks is a reasonable commitment. The live evening piece is fine for me — I'm remote so I don't have a commute eating into my evenings. I think if I were hybrid or in-office I might feel more fatigue around a weeknight session, but for my current setup it actually works pretty naturally. The project work component fits well because I can tie it directly to things I'm already working on, which means it doesn't feel like extra work so much as parallel work. I'd probably want to know which evening of the week, just for scheduling purposes, but the overall format works for me.
v.Q9: I think it would, yeah. Maybe not immediately — I'm not expecting a salary bump the week I finish — but in terms of positioning myself as the person who gets AI in an ops context, that has real career value. Operations is one of those functions where AI has a lot of practical leverage, and if I can demonstrate that I've formalized that knowledge and have a credential to back it up, that puts me in a stronger position when I eventually look for my next role or try to move into a more senior position. Job security is also a real consideration — I think the roles that disappear are the ones where people don't adapt, and having concrete proof that I've invested in adapting matters.
v.Q10: The framing lands for me personally, but I think it might land differently depending on who's reading it. I'm already pretty motivated so the fear angle doesn't really move me either way — it's more of a neutral statement of reality. What would resonate even more for me is something around building a competitive edge rather than avoiding a penalty. Like, framing it as 'here's what you can do that you couldn't before' feels more energizing than 'don't get left behind.' But I recognize that the fear framing probably does motivate some people who need that push, so I'm not saying it's wrong — just that for someone already engaged, the opportunity framing is more exciting.
v.Q11: I would have guessed somewhere between fifteen hundred and twenty-five hundred, so three thousand is at the higher end of what I expected. My honest reaction is that it's not a deal-breaker but it would almost certainly require employer sponsorship for me to pull the trigger. Self-funding three thousand dollars is a real ask, and I'd want to feel very confident in the ROI before I did that out of my own pocket. If I could get my company to cover it as a professional development expense — which I think is possible — then three thousand actually feels like a reasonable amount for a university certificate with structured instruction. It's in the range of a professional conference or a certification program, so it's not wildly out of line. But without employer backing, I'd hesitate.
v.Q12: Employer covered, ideally. We have a professional development budget — it's not huge, maybe a thousand to fifteen hundred per person per year — so three thousand would probably require a special request or an exception. I think I could make the case for it, especially given the informal AI-champion role I've kind of taken on. If it came down to splitting it, I'd consider contributing a portion, maybe up to five hundred or so out of pocket. But if my employer said no entirely, I'd probably hold off and look for something more affordable rather than fully self-fund at that price.
v.Q13: The main barriers are the price and the depth question. If I spend eight weeks on something and find out the material is too introductory for where I already am, that's a real frustration. I'd want some kind of signal upfront — a curriculum preview or skill assessment — that tells me whether this is the right level for me. The employer approval process is also a real barrier, just logistically. Even if my manager is supportive, getting a three-thousand-dollar exception approved through finance takes time and effort. And timing matters — if cohorts only run a couple of times a year and I miss the window, I might lose momentum.
v.Q15: A clearly visible curriculum breakdown with module-level detail, so I can see whether the content is going to push me or just cover things I already know. That transparency would answer my biggest hesitation directly and probably move me from likely to very likely without needing anything else to change.

v.Q2:
It shows up in a few places, but I'd describe myself as an occasional user rather than someone who's really integrated it into my workflow. I've used ChatGPT for content drafts — product descriptions, email campaign copy, some internal communications — and my team has used it similarly. We recently got a trial of a tool called Jasper that's positioned for marketing specifically, and we tested it for a campaign brief process, though I haven't made a decision on whether to keep it.

The honest challenge in manufacturing marketing is that a lot of our content is highly technical, and the AI-generated drafts often need significant editing to be accurate, which somewhat eats into the time savings. So I find it useful for starting points and structure but less useful for finished product, at least in my specific context. There is some pressure internally — our VP of Marketing mentioned on a team call a few months ago that she wants us to show how we're incorporating AI into our processes, though it was more of a nudge than a directive. I feel like I need to be more systematic about it rather than just dipping in when it's convenient.

I did a HubSpot certification on my own time, which was free and honestly pretty good for what it was. A couple of years ago I spent about two hundred dollars on a digital strategy course through a smaller online platform, which I'd describe as a mixed experience — the content was okay but I drifted away from it because the format was fully self-paced and I just lost momentum.

What makes me invest is direct applicability and, increasingly, whether there's a real credential at the end. After nine years in marketing I've accumulated a lot of informal knowledge and I feel the absence of a strong formal credential sometimes, particularly when I'm competing with people who have MBAs or formal certifications in areas I've just learned on the job. The barriers are time and relevance in roughly equal measure. Managing a team means my schedule is less predictable than it was as an individual contributor.
